title: Teaching on Purpose #18 No opt out
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In this installment of his Teaching on Purpose series, Adam Kohlbeck takes the purpose "checking for understanding" and argues that teachers rarely specify what exactly they want to check. Drawing on a podcast conversation with Chiltern Learning Trust EdTech lead Christian Turton, he distinguishes checking the depth of understanding of one or two pupils from checking the headline understanding or key misconceptions of the whole class. He walks through three techniques matched to three aims. "No opt out" turns an "I don't know" into a diagnostic sequence of asking peers and then returning to the first student. A tech-supported variant with a multiple-choice question and free-text box keeps the rigour while removing the anxiety of public questioning. A four-option question with misconception-coded distractors checks for specific errors. His conclusion is that technique should be chosen by purpose: the right thing at the right time for the right reason.
points: "Checking for understanding" covers two different aims, depth for a few pupils and breadth for the whole class, and treating them as the same thing leads to poorly matched techniques.
No opt out works as a diagnostic: after peers answer, asking the original student to judge which answer is correct shows whether they understood or were simply inattentive.
When public questioning provokes anxiety, a tweak that keeps the requirement to articulate thinking, such as anonymous free-text responses on devices, preserves rigour while lowering the barrier.
Multiple-choice questions can check for specific misconceptions when the wrong options are deliberately built from likely errors, as in the Year 1 "which is not an animal" example.
The through-line is that technique selection should follow purpose, so that teachers do the right thing at the right time for the right reason.
quotes: My hunch is that we probably don’t pay enough attention to precisely what we care about in the context of student understanding. This is something I explored with Christian on the podcast but in short, there is a trade-off to be made between breadth and depth.
Do we want to check the depth of understanding of a few pupils or even just one pupil… or is it more important that we check the headline understanding of the whole class?

The technique kicks in when you ask a student a question and they reply with ‘I don’t know’. At that point, the teacher asks another student before returning to the first student and asking them the same question again.
If they are able to compare the two responses from their classmates and decide which is the best, this tells the teacher that they probably do understand.

In this example, we have removed the barrier of the anxiety being triggered by being asked to articulate understanding publicly. But, we have preserved the key ingredient of the original technique – the requirement to articulate a depth of thinking.
The two incorrect answers are not chosen at random. They are chosen because of the likely misconceptions that are baked into them.
So, when it comes to Checking for understanding, as with all teaching decisions, even we are driven by the same purpose, it’s about doing the right thing at the right time for the right reason.
